comments.author: @roamingdev
comments.text: Thanks for the video, Nate! In 15:39, you mentioned that it is best to reference other MD files from the CLAUDE.md file using the @ symbol to save tokens. According to the docs: "CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using @path/to/import syntax. Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them". That means all files will be loaded into context when the session starts. If you want to avoid loading them, referencing them without the @ symbol will skip loading them into the context.

comments.text:
Well. Okay. This is a mix of impressive engineering and a huge red flag. Here's the breakdown:

The Impressive Part (from a technical standpoint):
The dude built a working MCP server that spins up a Kali Linux container on-demand. That's clever. The containerized approach (starting when needed, disappearing when done) is actually a smart way to isolate potentially dangerous tools. From a purely technical angle, it's a neat integration.


Okay but now the HUGE RED F***ing FLAG:


They just gave an AI direct, automated access to Kali Linux tools. Kali isn't inherently malicious (it's a legitimate penetration testing distribution used by security professionals) but it contains a vast arsenal of tools that can absolutely be used for illegal activity (network scanning, vulnerability exploitation, cracking f***ing passwords, etc.).

The casual "Let's see what it can do, whoop de f***ing doo!" followed by "Scan this network!" and "Hack this web application!" without any mention of authorization, scope, or legal boundaries is where this goes from "cool demo" to "potential g*dd*mn felony."



The Core Problem:
Even if the intent was educational or for testing their own systems, an AI doesn't understand context, ownership, or legal boundaries unless explicitly programmed with those constraints. Giving it the capability to launch attacks without robust safeguards is like handing a loaded gun to someone who doesn't understand the concept of "target" or "backstop."



This is exactly why tool access for AI needs to be designed with extremely careful scoping, user authentication, audit logging, and hard-coded ethical constraints. The MCP toolkit is powerful, but power without responsibility in cybersecurity is a recipe for disaster.



Bottom line: Cool tech demo, but the lack of any mention of authorization, legal boundaries, or safeguards makes this a textbook example of how NOT to deploy AI with powerful offensive capabilities.
